memory_candidates.content: On a shared git tree with concurrent sibling dispatches, bash .claude/scripts/deploy-headless.sh's inline verify step auto-runs generate-context-line-counts.sh --write as a side effect of every redeploy. This rewrites index-entries.json's line_count for EVERY stale entry repo-wide, not just the caller's own files -- including entries belonging to concurrently-active sibling tasks' own in-flight edits. If you need a fresh deployed tree mid-task (e.g. to test a new script against generate-task-order.sh or run verify-deploy.sh), expect this and reconcile afterward: capture `git show HEAD:<path>` as the baseline, re-apply only your own intended entries' corrections programmatically, and verify via `git diff --stat` before every commit that touches that file. Never trust whatever deploy-headless.sh/verify-deploy.sh happens to leave sitting in the working tree.

For a script that must regenerate a mechanically-derived section of a file while retaining human-authored content elsewhere in the same file, a robust and simply-testable design is full-file reassembly from extracted section bodies (one function per authored-verbatim section plus the regenerated ones), rather than literal in-place line-splicing. Each authored section is captured verbatim via a header-to-next-header awk extraction and re-emitted unchanged; only the generated sections are rebuilt. This made byte-identical retention and idempotency trivial to verify (diff/md5sum against a live file in --dry-run mode) and caught a real bug early: a free-floating authored paragraph living after the last fenced block in an otherwise-generated section was silently dropped by the first implementation, found only by testing --regenerate --dry-run against the real live file rather than only synthetic fixtures.
